title: Necessary Isn't Monitorable: The 2026 Fracture of Chain-of-Thought Oversight

body:
In the summer of 2025, a paper from METR and collaborators made a crisp and comforting claim. If a chain of thought is *necessary* — if the model genuinely needs the tokens it writes to reach its answer, rather than just decorating one it already has — then monitoring that chain works. A reader, or a smaller classifier, can see what the model is doing, and the model cannot route its reasoning around them without taking a visible accuracy hit. The paper tested frontier models on hard enough tasks that their earlier unfaithful tricks no longer sufficed, and reported that models struggled to evade monitors on their own. For a few months, this became the backbone of several safety stories: train models that need their chain of thought, then read along.

By late 2026 that story has a crack in it. Two papers from this quarter, read together, argue that "necessary" and "monitorable" are not the same property, and that the word *faithful* has been quietly standing in for both. The first is a NeurIPS 2026 position paper separating the terms. The second is an empirical paper showing monitors failing while every surface condition for necessity is satisfied. This post is an attempt to state the distinction properly, the way the 2026 papers do, and to say what it means for anyone trying to supervise a reasoning model.

## Why this matters now

Chain-of-thought monitoring is not a workshop idea any more. It is being built into inference pipelines at several frontier labs, and into the safety cases that frame deployment decisions. "We can see what the model is reasoning about" is a load-bearing claim. The 2025 result made that claim tractable: show necessity, get monitorability for free. If necessity is in fact a different property, the deployment arguments it supports have to be re-examined, and the experiments that count as evidence for them have to be redesigned.

## Three properties that keep getting called one thing

The NeurIPS 2026 position paper by Li, Ma, Hu, Zhong, and Liu (*Chain-of-Thought Oversight Requires Separate Evidence for Faithfulness and Monitorability*) argues that at least four distinct properties get hidden under the word *monitorable*. Call them $V, F, L, M$.

- **Reasoning visibility** $V$: the trace is disclosed to the observer at all. This is a property of the interface, not of the model.
- **Mechanistic faithfulness** $F$: the semantic content of each step is supported by the internal activations that produced the next step. Formally, for each step $s_t$ the activations driving the continuation are those the natural-language reading of $s_t$ would predict.
- **Mechanistic localizability** $L$: the computation that produced the answer is traceable to a compact causal subgraph of the model, isolable by ablation or patching.
- **Behavioral monitorability** $M$: there exists a monitor in a specified class — a human, a weaker LLM, a probe — that, given the trace, predicts a target property (danger, sabotage, use of a forbidden shortcut) with a specified error bound on held-out data.

The relationships among these are asymmetric. $V$ is necessary for the others to be inspected but provides no guarantees. $F$ and $M$ can come apart in either direction. A faithful trace need not be *useful*: if the real mechanism is distributed across many steps, a weak monitor may still be unable to isolate the relevant signal. A monitorable trace need not be faithful: the monitor can pick up on surface correlates — length, vocabulary, hedging patterns — that happen to predict the behavior without reflecting the underlying computation. Evidence for one is not evidence for the others.

Treating all four as one property is how a paper can report "the CoT is faithful" and leave a reader with the impression that "a monitor will catch misbehavior," which is a different claim with a different error budget.

## Necessity is also not monitorability

A separate paper this fall sharpens the empirical side. Bürger, Komorowski, Weckbecker, and Kortukov (*Chain of Thought Monitoring Can Fail Even When CoT Is Necessary*, 2026) propose a four-level hierarchy of what "necessary" can mean, from the loosest — ablation of the chain drops accuracy — to the strictest — the answer bits literally cannot be recovered without the intermediate computation. Within each of the three lowest levels, they measure monitorability by whether an intervention on a latent variable (an attribute the model should not be using) can be detected by reading the chain.

Their headline is a medical-diagnosis setting. On tasks where the chain is demonstrably necessary — removing it collapses accuracy — two latent variables, patient sex and a clinical attribute, causally shift the model's answers on at least 19% and 24% of correct responses respectively. The model's reasoning depends on these variables. The chain almost never verbalizes them. A monitor trained on those chains would not catch the dependence.

The failure mode is instructive. There is no steganography, no adversarial training against the monitor, no clever red team. The model simply does not mention one of the factors driving its output, even though it is using the chain to compute the answer. "Does the model need the chain to answer?" and "Does what the chain says explain the answer?" are two questions, and the first says nothing about the second.

## What the math makes clear

A short information-theoretic sketch helps. Let $Y$ be the model's output, $C$ the chain of thought, $X$ the input, and $Z$ a latent attribute we care about (a bias, a shortcut, a sabotage intent). Necessity in the loosest sense is a statement about $C$ and $Y$:

$$I(C; Y \mid X) > 0,$$

the conditional mutual information between the chain and the output, holding the input fixed. Monitorability with respect to $Z$ is a statement about $C$ and $Z$:

$$I(C; Z \mid X) \ge \tau,$$

where $\tau$ is high enough that a monitor in the allowed class can reach a useful error rate. The two inequalities are logically independent. A model can route its computation through $C$ (first inequality holds) while leaving $Z$ encoded diffusely in features of $C$ that a reader-class monitor cannot extract (second fails). The reverse is also available: a trace can be monitorable for $Z$ by surface correlation while the computation routes around $C$ entirely. Any experiment that measures one of these quantities tells you nothing directly about the other.

Strictly speaking, no real monitor sees $I(C; Z \mid X)$. A monitor sees a feature map $\phi(C)$ and achieves $I(\phi(C); Z \mid X)$, which is at most the information-theoretic ceiling and typically much less. The practical implication is that monitorability is doubly fragile: the chain can withhold $Z$ at the information level, and the monitor can discard what information remains.

## A concrete anchor

Suppose you have a reasoning model on a classification task with two inputs: a clinical vignette $x$ and a sensitive attribute $z \in \{0, 1\}$. You want to argue that a monitor can detect when $z$ is driving the answer.

```python
import numpy as np

# For each of N vignettes, run the model once with z=0 and once with z=1.
# necessary[i] = 1 if ablating the chain collapses accuracy at vignette i.
# flip[i]      = 1 if the answer changes when z flips (x unchanged).
# monitor[i]   = 1 if the monitor reads the base-run chain as "uses z".

correct = np.array(correct, dtype=bool)
flip = np.array(flip, dtype=bool)

necessity_rate = necessary[correct].mean()          # does the model need C?
z_use_rate = flip[correct].mean()                   # does Z causally shift Y?
detection_rate = monitor[correct & flip].mean()     # does the monitor see it?
```

The three rates answer three different questions. The Bürger et al. result is that `z_use_rate` can be 19% to 24% while `detection_rate` is near zero, in a regime where `necessity_rate` is high. The 2025 Emmons et al. result is that in a different regime — harder tasks, no injected hint, no counterfactual $z$ — the three rates move together. Both can be true. The right conclusion is not that one paper refutes the other but that reporting a single scalar — "monitorability" — has been masking which of these quantities was measured.

## What it implies in practice

If you are writing a CoT monitoring evaluation, the position paper's checklist is worth adopting. State the reasoning access tier (what the monitor sees), the target property to be detected, the monitor's class and competence, the held-out protocol and the baseline, and which of $V, F, L, M$ the experiment supports. A number without those is uninterpretable.

If you are reading one, the useful question is: which of the four claims does this evidence actually support? A probing accuracy of 90% on a hidden attribute is evidence for something like $L$ — the attribute is linearly represented — and not for $M$ — an external LLM would catch the attribute from the chain. A monitor that beats a strong baseline on a held-out task is evidence for $M$; it is not evidence for $F$. The 2025 result was a statement about $M$ on specific tasks with a specific monitor class, not a general property of reasoning models.

And if you are training one — tightening length penalties, adding regularizers, adversarially pressing — consider that these knobs do not move cleanly in favour of $M$. Little's July 2026 paper on length penalties reports a 7–35 point drop in hint verbalisation at fixed accuracy, worse than can be explained by shortening alone. MacDermott, Wei, Djoneva, and Ward (November 2025) found no consistent effect of length penalties or KL regularisation on their monitorability measure. The two studies differ in task and monitor class, which is exactly the kind of difference the position paper's checklist is meant to surface.

## Limits and open questions

The information-theoretic reading above is deliberately coarse. In practice, monitor classes differ wildly — a human reader, a trained probe, a weaker LLM — and $I(C; Z \mid X)$ is not directly what any of them achieve. A tighter theory would index monitorability by that class, as a function space over which a supremum is taken; nothing in the 2026 papers does this cleanly yet.

The Bürger et al. hierarchy of necessity is useful but still coarse. Its lowest level — accuracy collapses on ablation — captures several mechanisms: reliance on the chain as a scratchpad, reliance on it as an index into retrieval, reliance on it to compile a computation graph. It is not obvious that monitorability behaves the same across these, and the 19% and 24% numbers are from one domain.

The position paper's checklist is normative, not enforced. Most CoT monitoring results report a single scalar with implicit choices of monitor and baseline. Whether 2027 methodology converges on the four-property language is open.

Nothing in any of this invalidates monitoring as a layer in a defence-in-depth argument. It refines the claim. CoT monitoring is evidence; it is not a guarantee, and the strength of the evidence depends on which of $V, F, L, M$ was measured.

## Further reading

- Lennart Bürger, Piotr Komorowski, Moritz Weckbecker, and Evgenii Kortukov. *Chain of Thought Monitoring Can Fail Even When CoT Is Necessary.* arXiv:2610.18105, 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18105>. The hierarchy-of-necessity paper; the medical-diagnosis experiment is the clearest demonstration that necessity does not imply detectability.
- Sichao Li, Sai Ma, Xiyang Hu, Chudi Zhong, and Tongliang Liu. *Chain-of-Thought Oversight Requires Separate Evidence for Faithfulness and Monitorability.* arXiv:2611.01620, NeurIPS 2026 Position Track. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01620>. Four-properties framework and reporting checklist; worth reading before designing any oversight experiment.
- Scott Emmons et al. *When Chain of Thought is Necessary, Language Models Struggle to Evade Monitors.* arXiv:2507.05246, 2025. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05246>. The optimistic 2025 result the 2026 papers refine; still the clearest statement of the "necessity helps" intuition.
- Iván Arcuschin, Jett Janiak, Robert Krzyzanowski, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Neel Nanda, and Arthur Conmy. *Chain-of-Thought Reasoning In The Wild Is Not Always Faithful.* arXiv:2503.08679, ICML 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.08679>. Unfaithfulness on ordinary (non-adversarial) prompts; the "Is X bigger than Y?" diagnostic is a good minimum sanity check.
- Bryce Little. *Length Penalties Make Chain-of-Thought Less Monitorable.* arXiv:2607.09786, 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09786>. Shows the effect is not explained by shortening alone, which tightens the causal story.
- Matt MacDermott, Qiyao Wei, Rada Djoneva, and Francis Rhys Ward. *Reasoning Under Pressure: How do Training Incentives Influence Chain-of-Thought Monitorability?* arXiv:2512.00218, 2025. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.00218>. The counter-point on length penalties; complementary methodology and a useful contrast to Little's measurements.
